Guessing a Column's Type

guess-data-type.Rmd

When you open a messy data file, two questions come up before you can do anything useful with a column:

  1. What is this? Are these dates, dollar amounts, county codes, people’s names?
  2. How do I store it without breaking it? If you save 06037 to a CSV and reopen it in Excel, it becomes 6037 — the leading zero is gone and the county code is ruined.

formex answers both. guess_data_type() tells you what a column is, and fx_stabilize() puts it in a form that is safe to store and reopen. This guide walks through both for a first-time user.

Guessing what a column is

Point guess_data_type() at a column of values and it returns a $route — its best read of what the column is:

guess_data_type(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021"))$route[
  c("data_type", "semantic_family", "semantic_type", "format_style",
    "depth", "confidence")]
#> $data_type
#> [1] "temporal"
#> 
#> $semantic_family
#> [1] "date"
#> 
#> $semantic_type
#> [1] "calendar"
#> 
#> $format_style
#> [1] "calendar"
#> 
#> $depth
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> $confidence
#> [1] 1

The answer is a path, from coarse to fine:

data_type  ›  semantic_family  ›  semantic_type  ›  format_style
 temporal        date              calendar          mdy_slash

Read it left to right: these values are temporal, specifically a date, a calendar date, written in month/day/year with slashes.

It only answers as far as it’s sure

The most important thing to understand is that guess_data_type() stops at the deepest level it can defend and does not force a guess. The depth field says how far it got:

0  I don't know          3  the specific type (e.g. calendar)
1  the broad data_type   4  the exact written format (a leaf)
2  the family

A column of clean dates resolves all the way to a leaf (depth 4). A column of bare five-digit numbers might only reach number (depth 1), because 12345 could be a count, a ZIP, or an ID — the values alone cannot say. That is the right answer, not a failure: a confident-sounding wrong guess is worse than an honest “this far and no further.”

# nothing matches -> depth 0, confidence low
guess_data_type(c("apple", "banana", "cherry"))$route$depth
#> [1] 3

How the guess is made, in two steps

You do not need to operate these, but it helps to know what is happening:

  1. Sample. On a big column it looks at the distinct non-missing values (up to 100), not every row — so it stays fast.
  2. Router → verifier. A router proposes a short list of likely types. A verifier then actually tries each candidate’s recipe on your values and keeps only the ones that genuinely fit — and that also reject junk. A type that would accept anything (like “is a number”) cannot win a specific leaf; it truncates instead. This is why the answer is trustworthy rather than merely plausible.

When the values are ambiguous, the column name can help

Some values fit more than one type. If you also pass the column’s name, it is used as a tie-breaker:

vals <- c("06037", "36061", "48201", "17031")
guess_data_type(vals, name = "county_fips")$guess
#> [1] "county_fips"
guess_data_type(vals, name = "zip_code")$guess
#> [1] "zip_code"

Stabilizers: making a column safe to store

A stabilizer is the second half of formex. It takes the raw values and rewrites them into a stable form — one that survives being written to a CSV and reopened in R, Excel, or anything else without losing information and without being silently re-typed into the wrong thing. Think of it as putting the column into a protected state.

Here is the problem a stabilizer solves. Save these raw values and reopen them, and three things can go wrong:

raw value what a naive reopen does why it’s wrong
06037 (county FIPS) becomes the number 6037 the leading zero is dropped
3/15/2019 may become text, or the wrong date in another locale ambiguous day/month order
$2,300.00 stays as text "$2,300.00" you can’t do math on it

fx_stabilize() fixes each by (1) normalizing the value and (2) attaching an import rule that tells a reader how to bring it back as the correct type:

fx_stabilize(c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020"), "calendar")[c("stable", "import_rule")]
#> $stable
#> [1] "2019-03-15" "2020-12-31"
#> 
#> $import_rule
#> [1] "{{ as_yyyymmdd }}"
fx_stabilize(c("$2,300.00", "17,298$", "-45"), "usd")[c("stable", "import_rule")]
#> $stable
#> [1] "2300"  "17298" NA     
#> 
#> $import_rule
#> [1] "{{ default:numeric }}"
  • The date is normalized to unambiguous ISO 2019-03-15, which every tool reads the same way.
  • The dollar amounts become plain numbers you can compute on; the fact that they are USD rides along as metadata, not buried in the text.

For an identifier like a county FIPS, the stable value keeps its leading zero and carries the rule that re-imports it as text, so 06037 stays 06037 instead of collapsing to a number:

fx_stabilize(c("6037", "06037"), "geographic", "county_fips")[c("stable", "import_rule")]
#> $stable
#> [1] "06037" "06037"
#> 
#> $import_rule
#> [1] "{{ as_factor }}"

That import_rule is the key idea: a stabilized file is self-describing. Written alongside the data, it lets the next reader load each column back as the correct type automatically — dates as dates, codes as text, amounts as numbers — with no manual fix-ups and no silent corruption.

The whole loop 

x     <- c("03/15/2019", "12/31/2020", "01/01/2021")
route <- guess_data_type(x)$route          # 1. what is it?
fx_stabilize(x, route$semantic_type, route$format_label)$stable  # 2. make it safe
#> [1] "2019-03-15" "2020-12-31" "2021-01-01"

guess_data_type() says what a column is; fx_stabilize() puts it in a standard, protected form. A workflow package such as datagoodr builds on these two calls to profile a whole data frame, let a human confirm each column, and write out a cleaned, self-describing file. The shared vocabulary both calls speak is the subject of the Data-Type Ontology vignette; the detectors that do the recognizing are catalogued in the Data-Type Detector Guide.

For backward compatibility guess_data_type() also returns the older flat fields ($guess, $ontology, $confidence, $candidates) and score_data_type() still exposes the raw per-detector pass rates; new code should use $route.
